[[File:ArsenalTottenhamSat.png|300px|thumb|right|Satellite map of North London showing locations of Arsenal's old Highbury Stadium (red) and Tottenham's old White Hart Lane ground (white)]]
The '''North London derby''' is the meeting of the [[association football]] clubs [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] and [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]], both of which are based in [[North London]], [[England]]. Fans of both clubs consider the other to be their main [[List of sports rivalries|rivals]], and the derby is one of the most watched derbies in the world.<ref>{{Cite web|date=30 May 2011|title=50 Greatest Rivalries in World Football|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/714215-50-greatest-rivalries-in-world-football|access-date=22 December 2020|website=Bleacher Report}}</ref> Although the two teams first played each other in 1887, the rivalry did not begin until 1913 when Arsenal moved their ground to North London from [[Woolwich]], south of the River Thames.

As of 22 February 2026, 199 games have been played between the two teams since their first game in the [[English Football League|Football League]] in 1909, with 86 wins for Arsenal, 62 wins for Tottenham and 52 games drawn. When games played before both joined the Football League are included, 213 games have been played, with Arsenal winning 91, Tottenham 68, and 55 drawn.<ref name="Stat" />

Notable matches of the North London derby include the games in which Arsenal won the league at [[White Hart Lane]] in 1971 and their invincible campaign in 2004,<ref name="eccleshare">{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/football/2016/11/03/arsenals-best-ever-north-london-derbies-against-tottenham-ranked/ |title=Arsenal's best ever north London derbies against Tottenham: ranked |first=Charlie|last= Eccleshare |date=17 November 2017 |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] }}</ref> Tottenham beating Arsenal 5–0 at home in 1983 and Arsenal winning by the same score away in 1978, and Tottenham beating Arsenal 3–1 at the semi-final of the [[1990–91 FA Cup]], which they went on to win.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://talksport.com/magazine/features/2011-04-20/tottenham-v-arsenal-10-memorable-north-london-derbies |title=Tottenham v Arsenal: 10 memorable north London derbies |first=Craig |last=Bloomfield |date= 20 April 2011 |work=Talk Sport }}</ref> The highest-scoring game in the North London derby is the 5–4 win by Arsenal at White Hart Lane in November 2004.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/eng_prem/3988131.stm|title=Tottenham 4-5 Arsenal |date=13 November 2004 |work=BBC }}</ref> The fixture's top scorer is [[Harry Kane]] with fourteen goals, having overtaken [[Bobby Smith (footballer, born 1933)|Bobby Smith]] and [[Emmanuel Adebayor]], who have ten goals each.<ref name="topscorer">{{cite news|title=Harry Kane sets north London derby goalscoring record|date= 6 December 2020|url=https://www.bt.com/sport/news/2020/december/harry-kane-sets-north-london-derby-goalscoring-record|agency=Press Association |via=BT Sport |access-date=6 December 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.goal.com/en/news/kane-sets-all-time-north-london-derby-scoring-record-with-superb-/rl0di0hb4r7s1aqz7ymjboll2 |title=Kane sets all-time north London derby scoring record with superb strike for Tottenham against Arsenal|first=Andrew|last= Steel|work=Goal |date=6 December 2020 }}</ref> 

Arsenal play their home games at the [[Emirates Stadium]] in [[London Borough of Islington|Islington]], while Tottenham Hotspur are based at the [[Tottenham Hotspur Stadium]] in the neighbouring borough of [[London Borough of Haringey|Haringey]]. The two stadiums are 4&nbsp;miles (6.4&nbsp;km) apart.

==History==

===Early matches===

The first meeting between the two teams was a friendly on 19 November 1887, when Arsenal were located in [[Plumstead]] (then part of [[Kent]] but now in [[Greater London]]), and known as [[Royal Arsenal]]. The match, played at Spurs' ground at [[Tottenham Marshes]], was abandoned 15 minutes before it was due to end "owing to darkness" with Spurs won 2–1.<ref name="autogenerated1">{{cite web | url=http://www.topspurs.com/pre-8788.htm | title=Tottenham Hotspur in Friendly Matches - Season 1887–1888 | work=Topspurs | access-date=20 December 2006}}</ref> The first completed match between the two teams was held the following February in Plumstead; Tottenham could only field nine players, and were beaten 6–2.<ref>{{cite book |chapter-url= https://books.google.com/books?id=l67VDAAAQBAJ&pg=PT20 |title= Turf Wars: A History of London Football |first= Steve |last= Tongue |chapter= Chapter 1 Early days (1863-1899) |date= 19 August 2016 |publisher= Pitch Publishing |isbn= 9781785312489 }}{{Dead link|date=March 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> 

The two teams competed together in the [[United League (football)|United League]] starting in the 1896–97 season.<ref>{{cite book |first=Phil |last=Soar |title=Tottenham Hotspur The Official Illustrated History 1882–1995 |year=1995 |publisher=Hamlyn |isbn=0-600-58706-1 }}</ref> The first meeting in competition was on 2 November 1896. Arsenal won 2–1.

Another notable match was in 1898 played at the Spurs ground at [[Northumberland Park, London|Northumberland Park]]. The match with the then Woolwich Arsenal was attended by a record crowd of 15,000, and the refreshment stand collapsed when spectators climbed up onto its roof in the overcrowded ground, resulting in some injuries and prompting Spurs to start looking for a new ground. The next year the club moved a short distance to what would become known as the [[White Hart Lane]] ground.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/premier-league/tottenham-hotspur-spurs-white-hart-lane-farewell-goodbye-diego-maradon-johan-cruyff-a7733846.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220621/https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/premier-league/tottenham-hotspur-spurs-white-hart-lane-farewell-goodbye-diego-maradon-johan-cruyff-a7733846.html |archive-date=21 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=White Hart Lane has seen Diego Maradona and Johan Cruyff, but after 118 years Tottenham have outgrown it|first= Martin |last=Cloake |date=13 May 2017|work=The Independent }}</ref> The first League match between the clubs was in the [[Football League First Division|First Division]], on 4 December 1909; Arsenal won 1–0.<ref name="AFCRecords">{{cite web | url=http://www.arsenal.com/history/club-records/club-records | title=Records against Tottenham | work=Arsenal.com | access-date=20 December 2006}}</ref>

===Beginning of rivalry===
[[File:Arsenal-Spurs Kits.svg|thumb|left|The traditional first kits of Arsenal (left) and Tottenham Hotspur (right).]]
However, a proper rivalry between the two teams did not begin until 1913, when Arsenal moved from the [[Manor Ground, Plumstead|Manor Ground]], [[Plumstead]] to [[Arsenal Stadium]], [[Highbury]], just four miles from Tottenham's [[White Hart Lane]], a move resented and opposed by Tottenham as they considered Highbury their territory.<ref>{{cite book |title= Spurs: The Illustrated History |date=2003|first=Bob |last=Goodwin |publisher=Breedon Books Publishing Co Ltd |isbn= 978-185983-387-2 |page=30}}</ref>  The move made Arsenal Tottenham's nearest neighbours and thus began a natural local rivalry. The two teams first faced each other as north London rivals in a War Relief Fund friendly on 22 August 1914 at White Hart Lane. Although Arsenal were in the [[Football League Second Division|Second Division]] and Tottenham in the First, Arsenal won 5–1.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.topspurs.com/1415.HTM | title=Season 1914–1915 | work=Jim Duggan's Topspurs | access-date=5 January 2007 | archive-date=1 January 2007 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070101023851/http://www.topspurs.com/1415.htm | url-status=dead }}</ref> They would go on to meet regularly during [[World War I]] in the [[London Combination]], the regional wartime competition of the time.

The rivalry escalated in 1919 when, after [[World War I]], the First Division was to be expanded by two teams, and the League held a meeting of the clubs to decide the two clubs by means of a vote. 19th-placed [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]], who would otherwise have been relegated, were allowed to stay and thus they took the first of the two spots. The second spot could have been awarded to 20th-placed Tottenham, or [[Barnsley F.C.|Barnsley]], who had finished third in the Second Division, but Arsenal (along with four other clubs) also bid for the place, despite finishing sixth in Division Two (although an error in the calculation of goal average meant Arsenal had actually finished fifth, which was corrected by the Football League in 1980).<ref>{{Cite web
| url = http://www.arsenal.com/news/news-archive/arsenal-s-final-game-outside-top-flight
| title = Arsenal's final game outside top flight
| website = www.arsenal.com
| access-date = 28 February 2016
}}</ref>

After an endorsement by League president and chairman of [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] [[John McKenna]] on account of their longer membership of the League, Arsenal won the vote by eighteen votes to Spurs' eight (Barnsley got five, [[Wolverhampton Wanderers|Wolves]] four, [[Nottingham Forest F.C.|Nottingham Forest]] three, [[Birmingham City F.C.|Birmingham]] two and [[Hull City A.F.C.|Hull City]] one) and were thus elected to the First Division.<ref name="soartyler"/>  The decision infuriated Tottenham and their supporters. It has been frequently alleged that Arsenal chairman [[Henry Norris (businessman)|Sir Henry Norris]] used underhand dealings in order to bring this about, although nothing has been proven.<ref>These allegations range from political machinations to outright bribery. A detailed account of what facts are known can be found in {{cite book
| author=Spurling, Jon
| title=Rebels for the Cause: The Alternative History of Arsenal Football Club
| publisher=Mainstream
| year=2004
| isbn=978-1-84018-900-1
| chapter=Chapter Two: Sleaze and the Tory MP }}</ref> Tottenham themselves had been elected to join the Football League Second Division eleven years prior after finishing 7th in the [[1907–08 in English football|1907–08]] [[Southern Football League|Southern League]], but it involved entirely separate leagues that did not have automatic right to move between them.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablese/engsouthernleaghist.html | title=England - Southern League Final Tables | work=RSSF }}</ref> Tottenham were initially unsuccessful in their attempt to join the Football League, and only narrowly won election to the Second Division after [[Stoke City F.C.|Stoke]] resigned from the league for financial reasons.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BlVGrgEACAAJ|title=The Biography of Tottenham Hotspur |first=Julie|last= Welch |publisher=Vision Sports Publishing|date= 7 September 2015 |isbn= 9781909534506 |chapter=Chapter 5 - The Human Chain of Lightning }}</ref>

Despite the setback, Tottenham were soon promoted back into the top flight after taking the [[1919–20 in English football|1919–20]] Second Division title,<ref name="tottenham_fchd">{{cite web | url=https://www.fchd.info/TOTTENHH.HTM | title=Tottenham Hotspur | work= Football Club History Database | access-date=15 September 2007}}</ref> and the derby began to be regularly contested. The first fully competitive derby match after Arsenal's 1913 move to north London was a First Division match that finished 2–1 to Tottenham, on 15 January 1921 at White Hart Lane. The early matches between the two were noted for their bitterness - a particularly vicious match in September 1922 led to both clubs being censured by [[the Football Association]] and threatened with being forced to play behind closed doors.<ref name="soartyler">{{cite book |author1=Soar, Phil  |author2=Tyler, Martin  |name-list-style=amp |   title=The Official Illustrated History of Arsenal |   publisher=Hamlyn |   year=2005 | isbn=0-600-61344-5| page=40 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |   author=Goodwin, Bob |   title=The Pride of North London |   publisher=Polar Publishing |   year=1997 | isbn=1-899538-04-6| page=37 }}</ref>

Tottenham played in the Second Division between the periods of 1928 and 1933, as well as 1935 to 1950,<ref name="tottenham_fchd"/> which naturally led to a drop in the number of matches between the two clubs in this period and a cooling of passions. In 1935 Arsenal registered its biggest ever win over Spurs in a 6–0 rout away at White Hart Lane. This 6-0 result remains the biggest win by any team wherein the derby.<ref name=Stats>{{cite web|url=http://www.arsenal.com/history/club-records/club-records|title=Records against Spurs|website=Arsenal.com|date=19 May 2024 }}</ref><ref name=Stat>{{cite web|url=http://www.11v11.com/teams/tottenham-hotspur/tab/opposingTeams/opposition/Arsenal/|title=Tottenham Hotspur vs Arsenal|website=11v11.com|access-date=24 September 2023}}</ref> Relations between the two clubs improved somewhat after the [[Second World War]], after Tottenham allowed Arsenal to play their home matches at White Hart Lane while Highbury was requisitioned as an [[Air Raid Precautions|ARP]] station and subsequently bombed. The two sides met in the [[FA Cup]] for the first time in the [[FA Cup 1948–49|1948–49 season]], when Arsenal won a third round tie 3–0.<ref name=Stat />

===1950–present===
[[File:The second half... (5195057092).jpg|thumb|left|200px|Kick-off for the second half at the north London derby, 20 November 2010. Arsenal were 2–0 up at this point, but were beaten 3–2.]]
Since 1950, there has only been one season (that of [[1977–78 in English football|1977–78]]<ref name="tottenham_fchd"/>) where Tottenham and Arsenal have not been in the same division, meaning fixtures between the two are regular. This has maintained the rivalry to the present day and there have been many [[#Cup semi-finals and title deciders|notable matches]]. Several times the course of a title or the journey to a cup final has relied upon the outcome of a derby match. As with any major football rivalry, gloating and banter between the two sets of fans, many of whom work and even live together, is commonplace.  Players who transfer between the two teams receive a bad reception from their former fans; an example was defender [[Sol Campbell]],<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.fifa.com/worldfootball/clubfootball/news/newsid=1002460.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090125024047/http://www.fifa.com/worldfootball/clubfootball/news/newsid=1002460.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=25 January 2009|title=Crossing the divide|date=22 January 2009 |work=[[FIFA]].com|access-date=25 September 2009}}</ref> who was nicknamed "[[Judas Iscariot|Judas]]" by Tottenham fans after he crossed the divide in 2001.
[[File:Arsenal vs Tottenham*.jpg|thumb|right|180px|Arsenal's [[Theo Walcott]] and [[William Gallas]] of Tottenham in the North London Derby of November 2012 which Arsenal won 5–2.]]
Arsenal's [[Theo Walcott]], after picking up a knee injury in the 83rd minute of a [[FA Cup]] third round tie against Tottenham in January 2014, was pelted with a hail of coins and plastic bottles whilst coming off the field on a stretcher by Tottenham fans at the [[Emirates Stadium]]. Walcott subsequently made a gesture on the stretcher to the Tottenham fans which reflected, at that point in time, the 2-0 scoreline of the game which it finished as eventually. An investigation was eventually made with regard to the perpetrators of the incident by the authorities.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2014/01/04/theo-walcott-taunt-spurs-fans-2-0-fa-cup_n_4542002.html|title=Theo Walcott Taunted Tottenham Fans With '2-0' Hand Gesture During Arsenal's FA Cup Win (GIF/PHOTO)|website=Huffington Post.com|date=4 January 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-london-26014757|title=Police seek Arsenal v Spurs Theo Walcott coin-throwers|work=BBC News |date=3 February 2014 }}</ref>

On 30 April 2017, Tottenham beat Arsenal 2–0 in the final North London Derby at White Hart Lane.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/39682885 | title=Tottenham Hotspur 2-0 Arsenal | work=BBC Sport | access-date= 14 May 2017 }}</ref> This result guaranteed Tottenham finishing above Arsenal in the league for the first time in 22 seasons.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/soccer/2017/04/30/spurs-beat-arsenal-for-1st-finish-above-neighbor-in-22-years/101129194/ | title=Spurs beat Arsenal for 1st finish above neighbor in 22 years | work=USA Today | access-date= 14 May 2017 }}</ref> Tottenham would then achieve a streak of six consecutive finishes above their rivals (from 2016–17 to 2021–22). On 31 July 2025, the first North London derby was held outside of the United Kingdom at [[Kai Tak Sports Park]] in [[Hong Kong]] as part of their pre-season fixtures.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/articles/c2deg950wnko|title=Arsenal and Tottenham to play first north London derby outside UK in Hong Kong|date=March 31, 2025|website=BBC Sport}}</ref> The match was won by Tottenham.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.espn.co.uk/football/report/_/gameId/735610 |title=Tottenham beat Arsenal in first-ever north London derby outside UK |first=James |last=Olley |date=31 July 2025|work=ESPN }}</ref>

==Fans==
{{main article|Arsenal F.C. supporters|Tottenham Hotspur F.C. supporters}}
[[File:Tottenham fans singing to Sol Campbell.ogv|thumb|250px|Tottenham Hotspur playing Arsenal in the [[Premier League 2009–10|2009–10 Premier League]] at [[White Hart Lane]]. Tottenham fans are singing a chant, which condemns [[Sol Campbell]] and praises [[Ledley King]]. Sol Campbell had been targeted by Tottenham fans since he had moved from Spurs to their north London rivals in 2001.]]
Both Arsenal's and Tottenham's fan bases are multi-ethnic, due to the racial diversity in London. In 2002, Arsenal had 7.7% of their fans calling themselves non-white British, rising to 14% in 2008, the highest in the league in these fans surveys.<ref>{{Cite news
| url = https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/sport/football/1844962.stm
| title = Soccer violence declining say fans
| date = 27 February 2002
| newspaper = BBC
| access-date = 28 February 2016
}}</ref><ref name=2008survey>{{cite web |url=http://www.premierleague.com/staticFiles/67/f8/0,,12306~129127,00.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100107034336/http://www.premierleague.com/staticFiles/67/f8/0,,12306~129127,00.pdf |title=National Fan Survey 2007/08 Season|work=[[Premier League]] |archive-date=7 January 2010 |access-date=4 June 2019}}</ref> Around 9% of Tottenham fans were non-White in 2008.<ref name=2008survey /> Both clubs also have extensive fan bases throughout the UK and the rest of the world. Arsenal fans call themselves "[[Arsenal F.C. supporters|Gooners]]", a term that is derived from the club's nickname "[[Arsenal F.C.|Gunners]]", which is itself a reference to Arsenal's origins as a munitions factory team.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://worldsoccertalk.com/2010/11/15/origins-of-nicknames-for-20-premier-league-clubs/|title=Origins of Nicknames for 20 Premier League Clubs|website=World Soccer Talk.com|date=18 March 2016 }}</ref>

Tottenham fans call themselves "[[List of ethnic slurs#Y|yids]]". Due to the historical support from the [[Jews|Jewish]] communities in North and East London, Tottenham once had a significant number of Jewish fans; it was estimated that around 10,000 or a third of the club's fans in the 1930s were Jewish. Due to this historical association, fans of many other clubs from the 1960s onwards have directed [[Antisemitism|antisemitic]] chants at Spurs fans.<ref name=jc>{{cite web |url=https://www.thejc.com/life/spurs-and-the-jews-the-how-the-why-and-the-when-rd2vlg5l |title=Spurs and the Jews: the how, the why and the when |first1=Martin |last1=Cloake|first2= Alan|last2= Fisher|date=6 October 2016 |work=The Jewish Chronicle |access-date=30 June 2018}}</ref> Tottenham no longer has a greater number of Jewish fans than other major London clubs such as Arsenal (Jewish support for Arsenal started to increase in the 1930s); an estimate put the number of Jewish fans at Tottenham as at most 5%, about the same number as Arsenal, but the antisemitic chants against Tottenham fans persisted.<ref name=jc/> In an attempt to draw the sting from these chants, Tottenham fans (whether Jewish or not) adopted the words "yid" and "yiddo" for themselves and thereby turned a pejorative into a term of pride and belonging. There is, however, still some controversy over the use of "yid" or "yiddo".<ref>{{Cite news
| url = https://www.theguardian.com/football/2011/apr/14/kick-it-out-spurs-y-word
| title = Premier League tackles antisemitism with campaign to stamp out Y-word
| last = Gibson
| first = Owen
| date = 14 April 2011
| newspaper = The Guardian
| language = en-GB
| issn = 0261-3077
| access-date = 28 February 2016
}}</ref>
Tottenham are considered the club of North-East London in boroughs such as Haringey, Waltham Forest, Redbridge Enfield and Hackney, whereas Arsenal are more representative of North-West London in Islington, Camden, Brent, Harrow and Barnet.
A 2003 online survey found that Arsenal supporters most dislike Tottenham, and that Tottenham fans see Arsenal as their main rival.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.footballfanscensus.com/issueresults/Club_Rivalries_Uncovered_Results.pdf |title=RIVALRY UNCOVERED! |work=Football Fans Census |date=26 October 2011 |url-status=dead |access-date=2 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080910061502/http://www.footballfanscensus.com/issueresults/Club_Rivalries_Uncovered_Results.pdf |archive-date=10 September 2008 }}</ref>

Arsenal fans have a celebration day related to the north London rivalry called [[St. Totteringham's Day]], which is the day in the season when Tottenham cannot mathematically finish above Arsenal on the league table.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/8667734.stm | title=Sunday Football as it happened | work=BBC Sport | access-date=9 May 2010 | date=9 May 2010 | first=Jonathan | last=Stevenson}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2005/oct/21/thefiver.sport | location=London | work=The Guardian | title=Soprano and Jail Bird | first1=Barry | last1=Glendenning | first2=Paul | last2=Doyle | date= 21 October 2005}}</ref> Tottenham fans had long before declared 14 April to be St. Hotspur day in honour of Tottenham's 3–1 win over Arsenal in the 1991 FA Cup semi-final. St. Hotspur Day was also celebrated on 14 April 2010, when Tottenham beat Arsenal 2–1.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/teams/arsenal/7590558/Tottenham-v-Arsenal-as-it-happened.html | location=London | work=The Daily Telegraph | title=Tottenham v Arsenal: as it happened | first=Jonathan | last=Liew | date=14 April 2010}}</ref>

===Cup semi-finals and title deciders===
Although Arsenal and Tottenham have never met in a major cup final, there have been North London derby matches that have significantly contributed to one of the two clubs winning a trophy, such as semi-finals and title deciders. These include:

*'''Tottenham 0–1 Arsenal''' (3 May 1971): The final match of the [[1970-71 in English football|1970–71]] league campaign, with Arsenal needing a win or a goalless draw to take the [[Football League First Division|First Division]] title (a score draw would have meant [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]] won on [[goal average]]). The game was tight with few real chances on goal, until the very end. With three minutes to go, [[John Radford (footballer)|John Radford]]'s shot forced [[Pat Jennings]] into a good save; [[George Armstrong (footballer)|George Armstrong]] got to the rebound and chipped the ball across goal and [[Ray Kennedy]] headed home the winner. Spurs desperately tried to get a goal back but to no avail; Arsenal held on to win the title (the first half of [[Double (association football)|the Double]] that season).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/articles/2016/11/throwback-thursday-tottenham-vs-arsenal-may-3rd-19.html|title=Throwback Thursday: Tottenham vs Arsenal (May 3rd, 1971)|website=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste Magazine.com]]|date=2 November 2016 }}</ref>
*'''Tottenham 1–2 Arsenal''' (4 March 1987): Arsenal and Spurs had drawn 2–2 on aggregate in the [[EFL Cup|League Cup]] semi-finals; with no [[away goals rule]] in force, the match was replayed at Spurs' home ground of [[White Hart Lane]]. Spurs went 1–0 up through [[Clive Allen]] but Arsenal substitute [[Ian Allinson]] equalised and [[David Rocastle]] scrambled home the winner to send Arsenal through to the [[1987 Football League Cup Final|Final]], where they won their first trophy since 1979.<ref name="eccleshare"/>
*'''Tottenham 3–1 Arsenal''' (14 April 1991 at [[Wembley Stadium (1923)|Wembley]]): The first [[FA Cup]] semi-final between the two sides. Arsenal were chasing a second Double, but Tottenham's [[Paul Gascoigne]] scored after just five minutes with a [[Direct free kick|free kick]] from 30 yards out. [[Gary Lineker]] made it two, and although [[Alan Smith (footballer, born 1962)|Alan Smith]] pulled one back for the Gunners before half-time, Lineker scored again in the second half to seal the result.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/av/football/30579609 |title=FA Cup memories: Spurs-Arsenal in '91 |date=21 January 2015|work=BBC Sport }}</ref> Arsenal's Double dream was dashed, though they still won the League that season; Spurs lifted the Cup a month later. Known as St Hotspur Day for Tottenham fans.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://hotspurhq.com/2013/04/14/paul-gascoigne-stars-as-tottenham-defeat-arsenal-in-fa-cup-semi-final/ |title=Paul Gascoigne Stars as Tottenham Defeat Arsenal in FA Cup Semi-final |first= Logan |last=Holmes|work=Hotspur HQ }}</ref>
*'''Arsenal 1–0 Tottenham''' (4 April 1993 at [[Wembley Stadium (1923)|Wembley]]): The second FA Cup semi-final between the two, in which Arsenal sought revenge over their North London rivals for the 3–1 semi-final defeat two years earlier. [[Tony Adams (footballer)|Tony Adams]] scored with a header from a [[Paul Merson]] free kick for the Gunners in the 79th minute; Arsenal prevailed despite [[Lee Dixon]]'s sending-off, and went on to win the FA Cup in May and complete the first ever domestic cup double.<ref name="eccleshare"/>
*'''Arsenal 2–1 Tottenham''' (8 April 2001 at [[Old Trafford]]): The third FA Cup semi-final between the two. [[Gary Doherty]] gave Spurs the lead, before [[Patrick Vieira]] equalised for Arsenal. [[Robert Pires]] scored a second half winner to send Arsenal through to the first FA Cup final to be played outside England, where they lost 2–1 to Liverpool in [[Cardiff]].<ref name="eccleshare"/>
*'''Tottenham 2–2 Arsenal''' (25 April 2004): Arsenal were unbeaten in the Premier League and only needed a point to secure the title. The Gunners were 2–0 up after 35 minutes thanks to Patrick Vieira and Robert Pires' goals. A famous win looked to be on the cards, but Spurs restored some pride by denying Arsenal victory; in the second half [[Jamie Redknapp]] scored from long-range, then [[Robbie Keane]] converted a 90th-minute penalty to earn the draw. Arsenal thus won the title at their rivals' home ground for the second time.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/eng_prem/3628573.stm |title=Arsenal clinch title |work=BBC Sport |date=25 April 2004}}</ref>
*'''Arsenal 3–1 {{aet}} Tottenham''' (31 January 2007): Arsenal booked their place in the [[2007 Football League Cup final|2007 League Cup final]], for the first time since winning the competition in 1993, after this extra-time victory. The teams drew the first leg 2–2 at White Hart Lane where Tottenham threw away a 2–0 first half lead, eventually drawing the game. The return leg game was goalless until the 77th minute when [[Emmanuel Adebayor]] gave Arsenal the lead, before [[Mido (footballer)|Mido]] equalised for Tottenham five minutes from time. [[Jérémie Aliadière]] restored Arsenal's lead in the 105th minute and the game was eventually won by Arsenal after a 113th minute own goal by Tottenham's [[Pascal Chimbonda]], sending Arsenal through to the final, 5–3 on aggregate.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/league_cup/6305313.stm |title=Arsenal 3-1 Tottenham (agg 5-3) |first=Sam |last=Lyon |work =BBC Sport |date=31 January 2007}}</ref> Arsenal, however, would eventually lose the final to [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]].
*'''Tottenham 5–1 Arsenal''' (22 January 2008): Tottenham's first victory over Arsenal since November 1999, in the second leg of the [[2007–08 Football League Cup|League Cup]] semi-final; the teams had drawn 1–1 at the Emirates Stadium. Tottenham were 2–0 up by half time with [[Jermaine Jenas]]' strike and a [[Nicklas Bendtner]] own goal. After half-time, Spurs added two more from [[Robbie Keane]] and [[Aaron Lennon]]; [[Emmanuel Adebayor]] pulled one back for Arsenal, before [[Steed Malbranque]] scored a fifth goal in injury time to put Tottenham into the [[2008 Football League Cup final|2008 League Cup final]]. Spurs went on to lift the trophy.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/jan/23/match.arsenal | location=London | work=The Guardian | title=Five-star Spurs surge into Wembley final | first=Kevin | last=McCarra | date=23 January 2008}}</ref>
*'''Tottenham 2–1 Arsenal''' (14 April 2010): Spurs beat Arsenal 2−1 at White Hart Lane, goals by [[Danny Rose (footballer, born 1990)|Danny Rose]] and [[Gareth Bale]], to end the Gunners' hopes of winning the [[Premier League]].<ref>{{cite news | url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/eng_prem/8616181.stm | title=Tottenham 2-1 Arsenal | date=14 April 2010 }}</ref>

==Statistics and records==
[[File:North London Derby League Performance.svg|thumb|upright=1.4|Side-by-side comparison of Arsenal's and Tottenham Hotspur's final league positions 1894 to the present]]
As of 15 January 2025, there have been 197 competitive first-class meetings between the two teams since the first league meeting in 1909, of which Arsenal have won 84 and Tottenham 61.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.soccerbase.com/head2.sd?team2id=2590&team1id=142 | title=All time results between Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur | work=Soccerbase.com | access-date=15 September 2024 | archive-date=16 February 2007 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070216014801/http://www.soccerbase.com/head2.sd?team2id=2590&team1id=142 | url-status=dead }}</ref> The most goals in one game were scored in the closely contested 5–4 Arsenal victory at White Hart Lane on 13 November 2004. The biggest winning margin was a 6–0 away win by Arsenal on 6 March 1935. Tottenham have twice won 5–0 (25 December 1911 and 4 April 1983) and Arsenal once (23 December 1978), with all three fixtures taking place at White Hart Lane. Arsenal also won by 5–2 margins both in February and November 2012 home at the Emirates.<ref name="AFCRecords"/><ref name=Stat />

Tottenham's record for goals scored against Arsenal is 14 goals by Harry Kane, with [[Bobby Smith (footballer, born 1933)|Bobby Smith]]<ref name=topscorer /> scoring 10 goals followed by [[Billy Minter]] with nine goals.<ref name="mehstg">{{cite web | url=http://www.mehstg.com/arsefacts.htm | title=Spurs v Arsenal Facts | work=MEHSTG.com | access-date=20 December 2006 }}</ref> Arsenal's record is held jointly by [[Emmanuel Adebayor]], [[Alan Sunderland]] and [[Robert Pires]], with eight goals each.<ref name="Arseweb">{{cite web | url=http://www.arseweb.com/history/derbys.html | title=The North London Derby | work=Arseweb | access-date=12 March 2006 | archive-date=6 February 2006 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060206075811/http://www.arseweb.com/history/derbys.html | url-status=dead }}</ref> Adebayor also formerly shared the record for most goals by a player in the North London derby with ten: eight scored for Arsenal and two for Tottenham. Arsenal's long-time defender [[David O'Leary]] holds the record for most North London derbies played with 35, while [[Gary Mabbutt]] and [[Steve Perryman]] shared the corresponding record for Spurs, with 31.<ref name="Arseweb"/>

[[Terry Dyson]] is the only Spurs player to score a [[hat-trick]] in a first-class derby game, having done so on 26 August 1961 in a 4–3 win for Spurs.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.mehstg.com/arsestat.htm | title=Full results history of Spurs v Arsenal | access-date=27 June 2008 | archive-date=24 July 2008 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724183345/http://www.mehstg.com/arsestat.htm | url-status=dead }}</ref> The Arsenal players to have done so are [[Ted Drake]] (20 October 1934), [[Alan Sunderland]] (23 December 1978) and [[Eberechi Eze]] (23 November 2025).<ref name="Arseweb Tottenham"/>

==Crossing the divide==
Due to the rivalry between the clubs, relatively few players have played for both Arsenal and Tottenham since 1913. The first player to have played for both clubs, however, predated the start of the rivalry; [[Bill Julian]] joined Royal Arsenal in 1889 and Tottenham in 1894.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AOqcDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA237 |pages=237&ndash;238 |title=The Spurs Alphabet |first= Bob|last= Goodwin |publisher=Robwin Publishing House |date= 2017|isbn=978-0954043421}}</ref> Many other players played for both clubs before the start of the rivalry, including [[Charles Ambler (footballer)|Charles Ambler]], [[Arthur Elliott (footballer)|Arthur Elliott]], [[Thomas Fitchie]], [[Tom Pratt (footballer, born 1873)|Tom Pratt]], [[Peter Kyle (footballer)|Peter Kyle]], and [[George Payne (footballer, born 1887)|George Payne]]. A number of players had joined both clubs in the 20th century, but it was only in the 1960s that [[Laurie Brown (footballer)|Laurie Brown]] became the first player to have played in the North London Derby for both clubs.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/869096-adebayor-gallas-and-6-others-who-have-been-on-both-sides-of-the-n-london-derby#slide1 |title=Tottenham vs. Arsenal: The 8 Players Who Have Been on Both Sides of the Derby|first=Sean |last= Babcock|website=[[Bleacher Report]] |date=28 September 2011 }}</ref> The players who have played for both since 1919 when the rivalry escalated are listed below.<ref name="mehstg"/><ref name="Arseweb Tottenham">{{cite web | url=http://www.arseweb.com/teams/Tottenham.html | title=Arsenal vs. Tottenham | work=Arseweb | access-date=12 March 2006 | archive-date=3 April 2006 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060403112922/http://arseweb.com/teams/Tottenham.html | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.arsenal.com/history/profiles/548/tom-pratt|title=Tom Pratt|website=Arsenal.com|access-date=11 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151023201909/http://www.arsenal.com/history/profiles/548/tom-pratt|archive-date=23 October 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=Bio>{{cite web|url=http://www.fleetwoodtoday.co.uk/news/great-uncle-enjoyed-varied-soccer-career-1-1562128|title=Great-uncle enjoyed varied soccer career|website=Fleetwood Today.co.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.11v11.com/players/thomas-peet-pratt-47349/|title=Thomas Peet Pratt|website=11v11.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.11v11.com/players/george-clark-payne-47235/|title=George Clark Payne|website=11v11.com|access-date=29 September 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.11v11.com/players/peter-kyle-46176/|title=Peter Kyle|website=11v11.com}}</ref>

Former Arsenal winger [[Joe Hulme]] managed Tottenham Hotspur between 1945 and 1949. [[George Graham (footballer, born 1944)|George Graham]] was firstly an Arsenal player, then managed the Gunners between 1986 and 1994, before later taking up the reins at White Hart Lane between 1998 and 2001.

[[Clive Allen]] played three matches in Arsenal's 1980–81 pre-season friendly campaign, although never played a competitive league match for them.

[[Jamie O'Hara (footballer)|Jamie O'Hara]] was a youth player at Arsenal before joining Tottenham. However, he did not play a single game for Arsenal.<ref>{{Cite web
| url = http://www.arsenal.com/news/news-archive/wenger-campbell-wanted-to-play-for-titles
| title = Wenger - Campbell wanted to play for titles
| website = www.arsenal.com
| access-date = 28 February 2016
}}</ref>

[[Ron Piper]] was an amateur at Arsenal without playing a senior match before joining Tottenham in October 1960.

Tottenham all-time record goalscorer [[Harry Kane]], also the record scorer in North London Derby fixtures, briefly played for Arsenal's youth academy as an eight-year-old, being released after a single season.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/football/2018/02/12/liam-brady-arsenal-released-harry-kane-bit-chubby/ |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220111/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/football/2018/02/12/liam-brady-arsenal-released-harry-kane-bit-chubby/ |archive-date=11 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Liam Brady: Arsenal released Harry Kane because he was 'a bit chubby' |first=Daniel |last=Zeqiri |date=12 February 2018 |newspaper=The Daily Telegraph |access-date=9 July 2018}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

In addition, former Spurs player [[Herbert Chapman]] subsequently managed Arsenal from 1925 to 1934.<ref name=Herbert>{{cite web|url=http://www.arsenal.com/history/herbert-chapman/herbert-chapman-overview|title=Herbert Chapman - Overview|website=Arsenal.com|date=19 May 2024 }}</ref> Forward [[Billy Lane (footballer)|Billy Lane]] first played for Tottenham during 1922 and again from 1924 in a two-year stint at the club, but started in 1963 to feature as a scout for Arsenal.<ref>{{cite book |year=1999 |title=Official Matchday Magazine of Brentford Football Club versus Oldham Athletic 14/08/99 |location=Blackheath |page=27|publisher= Morganprint}}</ref> Former Gunner [[Terry Neill]] was Spurs's manager from 1974 to 1976, before he crossed back to manage Arsenal between 1976 and 1983.<ref name=Neill>{{cite web|url=http://www.arsenal.com/history/profiles/501/terry-neill|title=Terry Neill|website=Arsenal.com|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130802133532/http://www.arsenal.com/history/profiles/501/terry-neill|archive-date=2 August 2013}}</ref> 

[[Pat Holland]] was a reserve and youth team coach at Spurs from 1988 to 1995 and from 1997 to 2005 in a second spell with the club.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://m.tottenhamhotspur.com/news/pat-on-the-back-for-jamie-210303/|title=PAT ON THE BACK FOR JAMIE|website=Tottenham Hotspur.com|access-date=19 May 2017|archive-date=7 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107032327/http://m.tottenhamhotspur.com/news/pat-on-the-back-for-jamie-210303/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Holland went on to take up the role of a coach at Arsenal's Academy in 2012.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.arsenal.com/news/news-archive/holland-and-ampadu-join-arsenal-s-academy|title=Holland and Ampadu join Arsenal's academy|access-date=22 August 2012|publisher=Arsenal.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120823210108/http://www.arsenal.com/news/news-archive/holland-and-ampadu-join-arsenal-s-academy|archive-date=23 August 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> Holland left the role after less than two months for personal reasons, but has continued to feature for Arsenal as a scout.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mirror.co.uk/sport/football/transfer-news/arsenal-step-up-interest-10-4605928.amp|title=Arsenal step up interest in £10&nbsp;million-rated Ipswich left-back Tyrone Mings|date=10 November 2014|website=Mirror.co.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thescore.com/news/1264025/amp|title=Loan sharks: How English clubs are ruining their young talent|website=The Score.com|date=30 March 2017 }}</ref>

Sol Campbell's 2001 transfer from Tottenham to Arsenal was a landmark move at the time, with Campbell going on to win two Premier League titles and three FA Cups with Arsenal.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-04-29 |title=Sol Campbell's historic move from Tottenham to Arsenal |url=https://onefootball.com/en/news/sol-campbells-historic-move-from-tottenham-to-arsenal-38833373 |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=OneFootball |language=en}}</ref> Campbell was a club captain at Tottenham.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-04-29 |title=Sol Campbell's historic move from Tottenham to Arsenal |url=https://onefootball.com/en/news/sol-campbells-historic-move-from-tottenham-to-arsenal-38833373 |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=OneFootball |language=en}}</ref>

In its present format, Arsenal have, as of 2026–27, qualified to play in the [[UEFA Champions League]] on 23 occasions and Tottenham seven, although Tottenham did achieve a fourth-place finish in the [[2011–12 Premier League]] season but were denied a place in the Champions League due to Chelsea winning the Champions League. Arsenal were runners-up in both the [[2006 UEFA Champions League final|2005–06]] and [[2026 UEFA Champions League final|2025–26 Champions League]] seasons,<ref>[http://www.arsenal.com/news/news-archive/-we-re-proud-to-qualify-for-champions-league- Arsenal news archive] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160513100607/http://www.arsenal.com/news/news-archive/-we-re-proud-to-qualify-for-champions-league- |date=13 May 2016 }} Retrieved 4 September 2012</ref> as were Tottenham in the [[2019 UEFA Champions League final|2018–19 Champions League]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Tottenham 0 - Liverpool 2 |work=BBC Sport |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/48368443 |access-date=18 June 2019}}</ref> Prior to this, Arsenal qualified for the former European Cup on three occasions, while Tottenham did so once. Arsenal were unable to compete in the 1989–90 competition owing to a ban on English clubs following the [[Heysel Stadium disaster]].<ref>[http://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/english-football-clubs-banned-from-europe English clubs banned from Europe] Retrieved 18 November 2012</ref>

While the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup is recognised as the predecessor to the UEFA Cup, it was not organised by UEFA. Consequently, UEFA do not consider clubs' records in the Fairs Cup to be part of their [[UEFA#Competitions|European record]]. However, FIFA does view the competition as a major honour.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fifa.com/classicfootball/clubs/club=1903416/index.html |title=Classic Football: Clubs: FC Barcelona |publisher=FIFA |access-date=14 August 2014
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150429022457/http://www.fifa.com/classicfootball/clubs/club%3D1903416/index.html |archive-date=29 April 2015 |url-status=dead }}<br>{{cite web|url=https://www.fifa.com/classicfootball/clubs/club=31083/index.html |title=Classic Football: Clubs: AS Roma |publisher=FIFA |access-date=30 March 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150817060759/http://www.fifa.com/classicfootball/clubs/club%3D31083/index.html |archive-date=17 August 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
